Time: 3 min. Teaching intent: Set the evidence contract.
Talk track: A requirement table with measurable targets, owners, and missing values.
Expected answer / misconception: A named artifact with source and a check, not an unsupported opinion.
Visual: Input, reasoning, and evidence are separate.

Time: 3 min. Teaching intent: Retrieve prior knowledge before revealing the method.
Talk track: Is 'high bandwidth' a design requirement?
Expected answer / misconception: No. State an interface, target quantity, units, operating condition, and acceptance rule.
Visual: The three conditions identify what must be compared.
[Sources]
R2: IEEE EPS HIR 2024, Ch. 13: Co-Design | https://eps.ieee.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/HIR_2024_ch13_HIR_Co-Design.pdf

Time: 4 min. Teaching intent: Teach the mechanism or design rule.
Talk track: Bandwidth, power, size, cost, and reliability compete; a package choice only makes sense against stated targets. Trace the visual in order: system function; measurable target; package consequence. Connect this mechanism to the worked example: Synthetic example: a compute die beside four memory stacks needs a stated bandwidth and power budget before interposer size can be judged.
Expected answer / misconception: Ask students to explain the link between adjacent elements; a conceptual diagram is not a measurement.
Visual: Native diagram encodes the causal or design relationship.
[Sources]
R2: IEEE EPS HIR 2024, Ch. 13: Co-Design | https://eps.ieee.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/HIR_2024_ch13_HIR_Co-Design.pdf

Time: 4 min. Teaching intent: Work the example step by step.
Talk track: Set up the case: Synthetic example: a compute die beside four memory stacks needs a stated bandwidth and power budget before interposer size can be judged. Identify the starting information, state the reasoning step aloud, then ask what observation would check the conclusion. Stop before the next slide's question is answered.
Expected answer / misconception: Students must identify the input, the inference, and the check. 
Visual: Three-part reasoning path separates the example from its verification.
[Sources]
R2: IEEE EPS HIR 2024, Ch. 13: Co-Design | https://eps.ieee.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/HIR_2024_ch13_HIR_Co-Design.pdf

Time: 4 min. Teaching intent: Teach the mechanism or design rule.
Talk track: Count signal, power, ground, test, and spare contacts separately; a total pin count hides different physical demands. Trace the visual in order: signals; power / ground; test / spare. Connect this mechanism to the worked example: Synthetic worksheet: 800 signal connections plus 240 power/ground and 40 test contacts give 1080 assigned contacts, before routing margin. Boundary: The 1080-contact arithmetic is synthetic teaching data.
Expected answer / misconception: Ask students to explain the link between adjacent elements; a conceptual diagram is not a measurement.
Visual: Native diagram encodes the causal or design relationship.

Time: 3 min. Teaching intent: Pause for an individual answer, then reveal and discuss.
Talk track: Can 1080 contacts be treated as 1080 equivalent signal routes?
Expected answer / misconception: No. Power, ground, test, and high-speed signals impose different placement and return-path constraints.
Visual: The diagram lists the conditions to inspect without marking the answer.

Time: 4 min. Teaching intent: Teach the mechanism or design rule.
Talk track: Adjacency shortens some routes but may concentrate heat and make escape routing harder. Trace the visual in order: compute die; memory placement; routing / heat. Connect this mechanism to the worked example: Compare a close memory ring with a wider placement. The close layout may ease links while creating a hotter central region; neither wins without constraints.
Expected answer / misconception: Ask students to explain the link between adjacent elements; a conceptual diagram is not a measurement.
Visual: Native diagram encodes the causal or design relationship.
[Sources]

Time: 4 min. Teaching intent: Teach the mechanism or design rule.
Talk track: A stackup names each layer, material, interface, and thermal path; a cross-section is a design input, not decoration. Trace the visual in order: die / bumps; interposer or RDL; substrate / board. Connect this mechanism to the worked example: Trace one signal and one heat path through a proposed 2.5D stack. Mark every unknown thickness or conductivity rather than inventing it.
Expected answer / misconception: Ask students to explain the link between adjacent elements; a conceptual diagram is not a measurement.
Visual: Native diagram encodes the causal or design relationship.
